entry.title: Building an Invoice Approval Workflow with SAP Build Process Automation
entry.content:
A step-by-step guide to collecting invoice data through a form and routing it through a conditional, human-in-the-loop approval flow. 

Introduction 

One of the most common enterprise scenarios is: a document comes in, someone needs to review it, and a decision needs to be made. SAP Build Process Automation (BPA) is purpose-built for exactly this — orchestrating human approvals on top of business data, with no custom UI development required. 

In this post, we'll build a complete Invoice Approval workflow in BPA. An invoice form is submitted, a condition checks the total amount, and if it crosses a threshold, the invoice is routed to an approver's My Inbox as a read-only approval form with Approve/Reject actions. Once decided, an email notification is sent automatically. 

Here's what we'll cover: 

  • Designing a trigger form for invoice submission 
  • Building the process flow with a conditional branch 
  • Creating a read-only approval form for the reviewer 
  • Mapping data from the trigger form into the approval task 
  • Sending automated email notifications 
  • Configuring a mail destination for outbound email 
  • Testing the complete flow end to end 

Step 1: Create the Trigger Form (InvoiceFormSubmit) 

Every BPA process needs a way to start. Here, we use a Form Trigger — a form that, when submitted, kicks off a new process instance carrying whatever data was entered. 

  1. In your BPA project, add a new Form trigger and name it InvoiceFormSubmit. 
  1. Build out the fields to match your invoice structure: Invoice Number, Invoice Date, Due Date, Supplier, Bill To, Currency, and Purchase Order. 
  1. Add a Products Details table (a repeating list) with Description, Quantity, Unit Price, and Amount columns, so multiple line items can be captured. 
  1. Add Subtotal, Tax Amount, and Total Amount fields, followed by a Contact Details section (Name and Email) so we know who submitted the invoice and who should be notified later. 

 

 

The InvoiceFormSubmit trigger form being built in the Forms editor — Invoice Details section. 

 

 

The remainder of the form — Products Details, totals, and Contact Details, with the Submit button that triggers the process. 

With the form saved, this becomes the entry point for the entire process — every field here becomes a process variable we can use downstream. 

Step 2: Build the Process Flow 

With the trigger in place, switch to the process editor and lay out the flow logic. 

  1. Drag in a Condition step right after the trigger. 
  1. Add a branch condition: Total Amount is greater than 4000. This becomes the "If" path; everything else falls to "Default." 
  1. On the If path, add a User Task (the approval form) with two outcomes — Approve and Reject. 
  1. On the Default path (amount 4000 or below), add a Send Mail step for auto-approval, so low-value invoices skip manual review entirely. 
  1. After the approval task, branch again on the outcome: Approve goes to a Send Mail (approval) step, Reject goes to a Send Rejection Mail step. Both paths converge to the End event. 

 

 

The full deployed process: InvoiceFormSubmit trigger → Condition → ApprovalForm (with Approve/Reject branches) → email notifications → End. 

 

 

Configuring the branch condition — routing only invoices with Total Amount greater than 4000 to manual approval. 

Step 3: Configure the Approval Form 

The approval task is what actually shows up in the approver's My Inbox. It needs a Task Details section (subject, priority) and a Recipients section (who gets the task). 

  1. Open the ApprovalForm task and set the Subject to something dynamic, like "Invoice Approval for {Invoice Number}", so each task is identifiable at a glance. 
  1. Under Recipients, add the approver's email address (or a group) — this determines whose inbox the task lands in. 
  1. Set the Due Date type to Reference Date and bind it to the invoice's Due Date field. 

 

 

ApprovalForm task configuration — subject, recipients, and due date settings. 

Next, build the form UI itself. Rather than designing it from scratch, base it on the same layout as InvoiceFormSubmit, but make every field read-only — the approver should see the invoice clearly without being able to edit it. 

  1. Bind each field on the approval form to the corresponding output from InvoiceFormSubmit: Invoice Number, Invoice Date, Due Date, Supplier, Bill To, Currency, Purchase Order, and the Products Details list. 
  1. Bind Subtotal, Tax Amount, Total Amount, Name, and Email in the same way. 

 

 

Mapping InvoiceFormSubmit output fields into the ApprovalForm's inputs. 

 

 

Continuing the input mapping — Products Details bound as a list, plus Purchase Order, Subtotal, and Tax Amount. 

This mapping is what lets the approver see the exact invoice that was submitted, without any manual re-entry. 

Step 4: Configure the Approval Email 

Once a decision is made, the requester (or a stakeholder) should be notified automatically. 

  1. Add a Send Mail step on the Approve branch. 
  1. Set the To field by binding it to the Email field captured on the original form. 
  1. Set a dynamic Subject, such as "Invoice approval for Invoice No. {Invoice Number}". 
  1. In the Mail Body, greet the requester by name and include the key invoice details — Invoice Number, Supplier, Total Amount, and Currency — followed by a confirmation line. 

 

 

Building the approval email — binding process variables directly into the mail body. 

The same pattern applies to the Send Rejection Mail step on the Reject branch, just with different messaging. 

Step 5: Set Up the Mail Destination 

For BPA to actually send emails, it needs an outbound mail server configured as a Destination in your BTP subaccount — this is what BPA uses as the sender. 

Reference SAP Help Portal: Configure an SMTP Mail Destination-    
https://help.sap.com/docs/intelligent-robotic-process-automation/factory-user-guide/configure-smtp-mail-destination 

  1. In your BTP Cockpit, go to Connectivity > Destinations and create a new destination named sap_process_automation_mail (BPA looks for this name specifically). 
  1. Set Type to MAIL, Proxy Type to Internet, and Authentication to Basic Authentication with your mail account's credentials. 

 

 

The mail destination's main properties and authentication. 

  1. Add the required additional properties for an SMTP mail server: transport protocol, SMTP host and port, the from address, and the relevant TLS/SSL flags. 

 

 

Additional SMTP properties on the mail destination — host, port, TLS settings, and sender address. 

Once saved, this destination becomes the sender identity for every Send Mail step in the process. 

Step 6: Deploy and Test the Full Flow 

With everything wired up, it's time to release and deploy the project, then run it end to end. 

  1. Release and deploy the project. Copy the Form Link for InvoiceFormSubmit — this is the URL used to submit a new invoice. 
  1. Open the link and fill in a sample invoice — line items, totals, and a contact email — then hit Submit. 

 

 

Submitting a sample invoice through the InvoiceFormSubmit form. 

  1. Since the Total Amount exceeds 4000, the process routes to manual approval. Log in to My Inbox — the task appears with the invoice details already populated. 

 

 

The approval task in My Inbox, showing the read-only invoice details and Approve / Reject buttons. 

  1. Click Approve. The process resumes down the Approve branch and fires the Send Mail step. 
  1. Check the recipient's inbox — the approval email arrives with the invoice summary. 

 The approval email received in Gmail, confirming the invoice was approved. 

Wrapping Up 

🎉 That completes a full invoice approval workflow in SAP Build Process Automation — from form submission, through conditional routing and human approval, to automated email notification. 

What I found useful in this POC was how easily the individual BPA components fit together. The form collects the data, the condition applies the business rule, the approval form handles the human decision, and the email step communicates the result. Even though the example uses a simple invoice threshold, the same pattern can be extended to many other approval scenarios. 

In the next post, we'll look at combining this same approval pattern with SAP Document Information Extraction, so invoice data doesn't need to be entered manually at all — it gets extracted directly from an uploaded PDF.

entry.title: Connecting SAP Build Process Automation to a Trial Document AI Instance
entry.content:
Diagnosing a landscape mismatch between BPA and SAP Document AI on trial, and building a reusable extraction flow around it.

Introduction

In the first post of this series, we built an invoice approval workflow in SAP Build Process Automation, triggered by a manually filled form. The natural next step is to remove that manual step — read the invoice straight from a PDF and feed the extracted data into the same approval process.

That's exactly where this post started. But before we could get to the approval logic, we ran into a connectivity issue between BPA and SAP Document AI that's specific to trial landscapes. This post covers how we diagnosed it, the workaround that actually gets extraction working, and the one limitation that comes with it.

The Error

The first attempt was the obvious one: use BPA's built-in "Add a Document Template" wizard to register a template against our invoice schema. It failed immediately, before any real document was even involved.

 

SAP_IPA_28014 — the Document Information Extraction call fails with a 400 Bad Request, right at the template creation step.

Swapping the approach and trying the built-in Extract Data (Pre-Trained Model) activity directly against our sample invoice hit the same wall.

 

Extract Data (Pre-Trained Model) configured against a sample invoice PDF.

What Didn't Work

Our first instinct was that this was a subscription/entitlement glitch — a stale binding between the BPA and Document AI subscriptions. We re-subscribed both services from scratch a couple of times, on the theory that it would force a fresh landscape mapping. It didn't change anything; the same 400 kept coming back.

Finding the Actual Cause

The real answer came from comparing what URL the failing call was actually hitting against what our trial tenant's URL actually is.

The Test Console error for the built-in activity exposes the full request, including the URL it tried to call:

 

The built-in Extract Data activity was calling https://us10.doc.cloud.sap/document-information-extraction/v1/document/jobs.

Then we pulled the actual service key for our SAP Document AI trial instance from the subaccount's Instances and Subscriptions page:

 

SAP Document AI, subscribed under the trial subaccount alongside SAP Build Process Automation.

 

The service key's credentials show the real backend URL: https://us10-trial.doc.cloud.sap — not https://us10.doc.cloud.sap.

That's the mismatch. SAP Document AI base URLs follow the pattern https://<tenant-id>.<region>.doc.cloud.sap, and trial-tier URLs are distinguished by the -trial substring appearing in both the tenant and regional domain segments — while standard and premium plans map directly to the plain commercial landscape (us10, eu10, etc.). BPA's built-in Extract Data activities are resolving the endpoint from the region alone and dropping that -trial qualifier, so on a trial subaccount they always call a host that doesn't exist for our tenant. That explains the immediate 400, independent of anything about our schema, template, or document.

The Fix: a Destination-Based Extraction Flow

Since the built-in activities resolve the URL internally, there's no setting inside them to correct it. The workaround is to stop using those activities altogether and call SAP Document AI through an explicit BTP Destination instead, using a set of reusable Document AI activities that take the destination as a parameter rather than assuming a URL.

We built this on top of the approach and reusable automation package shared in Using Document AI Premium in SAP Build Process Automation, which packages a set of Document AI activities (extraction, capabilities, clients, schema lookup, job status, and Premium-specific calls) that go through a destination rather than a hardcoded region URL. The project and its GitHub repo are linked from that post.

  1. Create a Destination in the BTP Cockpit pointing to the correct trial URL — in our case https://us10-trial.doc.cloud.sap/document-information-extraction/v1 — using OAuth2ClientCredentials authentication with the Document AI service key's client ID and secret.

 

The Document_AI destination — Type HTTP, pointing at the correct -trial URL, authenticated via OAuth2ClientCredentials.

  1. Add the additional properties BPA needs to recognize and use the destination from within a process automation project — these enable it for use as a connector inside BPA and Build Apps.

 

Additional destination properties: sap.processautomation.enabled, BuildApps.Enabled, and related flags set to true.

  1. Import the reusable "Document AI service" package from the blog's GitHub project into your BTP workspace. It ships as a standalone Process Automation package with its own activities.

 

The imported (package) Document AI service project, with its released and editable versions.

One Limitation: Schema and Template Authoring

The package gives you activities to extract data and query schema/job status, but it doesn't give you a way to author a schema or a template from inside BPA. That part still has to happen in the standalone SAP Document AI UI, the same way it would for a non-trial setup.

  1. In the Document AI application, go to Schema Configuration and define your custom schema — header fields (Invoice Number, Dates, Supplier, amounts, etc.) and line item fields (Description, Quantity, Unit Price, Amount).

 

InvoiceApprovalSchema, defined directly in the Document AI UI — the same field structure used by the approval form in Post 1.

  1. Create a Template against that schema and validate it against a sample invoice, confirming the extraction confidence per field before relying on it.

 

InvoiceApprovalTemplate validated against a sample invoice — all header and line item fields extracted correctly.

Once the schema exists, the reusable package's extraction activity only needs the schema name and the destination — it doesn't need the template wizard that was failing earlier.

Building the Extraction Automation

With the destination and schema in place, the automation itself is straightforward: collect the PDFs from a folder, and for each one, call the package's extraction activity.

 

InvoiceApprovalAutomation — Get File Collection, then a For Each loop calling DocAI - Extract with Schema per file.

  1. Get File Collection reads every PDF from the source folder.

 

Get File Collection parameters — folderPath pointing at the invoice PDFs.

  1. Inside the loop, DocAI - Extract with Schema is called per file, passing the current file and the schema name (InvoiceApprovalSchema) created earlier — this is the activity from the reusable package, going through the destination rather than a hardcoded URL.

 

DocAI - Extract with Schema — fileToUpload bound to the current loop item, schemaName set to InvoiceApprovalSchema.

Testing Against Multiple Invoices

We ran the flow against three different sample invoices — different suppliers, currencies, and line items — to confirm the extraction held up beyond just the original demo document.

 

Test Console output — each invoice processed through the loop, with status DONE and the full extracted field set logged per file.

 

 

 

 

 

 

Three sample invoices (EUR and USD, different suppliers and line items) alongside their extracted JSON output — header fields and line items all mapped correctly.

Wrapping Up

With the destination-based package in place, extraction now works reliably against our trial Document AI instance — something the built-in BPA activities simply can't do on trial until SAP resolves the endpoint resolution on their side. The trade-off is one manual step: schemas and templates still need to be authored in the Document AI UI directly, rather than from within BPA.

 For the reusable package and destination pattern that this is built on — our part was tracing the actual root cause via the request URL, defining our own invoice schema, and wiring the extraction loop up as a standalone automation, tested end to end against multiple invoices.

With extraction now solid, the next step is the one this series set out to do from the start: feed this extracted data straight into the InvoiceApprovalProcess from Post 1, so a PDF landing in a folder ends up as an approval task in My Inbox with no manual form-filling at all.

entry.title: From Inbox to Folder: Fetching Gmail Attachments with SAP Build Process Automation
entry.content:
Connecting SAP Build Process Automation to Google Workspace, so invoice PDFs arriving in a Gmail inbox land in a local folder, ready for extraction and approval.

Introduction

This is the fourth post in the series. In the first post, we built the core invoice approval workflow in SAP Build Process Automation (BPA). In the second, we connected to a trial Document AI instance, and in the third, we wired extraction straight into the approval process. Throughout, the invoice PDFs were simply sitting in a folder, put there by hand.

In practice, invoices arrive by email. So in this post we remove that last manual step: a task automation connects to Google Workspace, searches a Gmail inbox for invoice emails, and saves the PDF attachments into a folder on the machine running the Desktop Agent. That folder is then what the extraction and approval flow reads from.

Here's what we'll cover:

  • Creating an OAuth 2.0 Client ID in Google Cloud Console
  • Creating the External Authentication in BPA Control Tower
  • Registering the authentication on the Desktop Agent and giving consent
  • Building a task automation that searches Gmail and downloads attachments
  • Testing it with a real email

Choosing How to Connect to Google Workspace

BPA offers a few ways to authorize against Google Workspace. Authorize Google (OAuth Client ID) and Authorize Google (Service Account) are activities placed inside the automation, and both work on Desktop Agent 2 and 3. Select Google Authentication works differently: the OAuth client is configured once in Control Tower, registered once on the Desktop Agent, and the automation simply selects it by name.

We'll use Select Google Authentication, which requires Desktop Agent 3 (SAP documents version 3.16 or higher for Google external authorization). No credentials live inside the automation itself, which keeps the project clean.

Step 1: Set Up the OAuth Client in Google Cloud Console

Everything starts on the Google side. Open the Google Cloud Console and select the project you want to work in. Under APIs & Services, the Credentials page shows the OAuth consent screen, the Create credentials button, and any OAuth 2.0 Client IDs already created.

 

APIs & Services > Credentials in the selected Google Cloud project.

  1. Enable the APIs. Under Enabled APIs & services, enable the Google Workspace APIs you plan to use. I enabled the Gmail API, Google Calendar API and Google Drive API. Only Gmail is used in this post, but the others save a trip back later.
  2. Configure the OAuth consent screen. On the Branding page of Google Auth Platform, give the app a name (mine is SAP-BPA-Test, which is what users see when they sign in) and a user support email.

 

Branding --- app name and user support email.

  1. Scroll down to the app domain fields and the developer contact email. The domain fields (home page, privacy policy, terms of service) can stay empty for a testing setup.

 

Branding, continued --- app domain, authorized domains and developer contact information.

  1. Set the Audience. I chose the External user type and left the publishing status as Testing. While in Testing, only listed test users can authorize the app, so add your own Gmail address under Test users.

 

Audience --- External user type, Testing status, and the test user list.

  1. Add scopes under Data Access. Scopes define what the app is allowed to do with the account. I added userinfo.email, cloud-platform, calendar, drive and the Gmail scope (https://mail.google.com/). Google groups Drive and Gmail under restricted scopes, which is why they get a stricter consent flow.

 

Data Access --- the non-sensitive, sensitive and restricted scopes added to the app.

  1. Create the client. Under Clients, create a new OAuth client with the application type Desktop app. I named mine Desktop Agent BPA. Google generates a Client ID and a Client secret, and you can also download them as a clientid.json file. Control Tower needs exactly these two values.

 

The Desktop client --- Client ID and client secret (sensitive parts hidden).

Treat the client secret like a password, and keep it out of screenshots and source control.

Step 2: Create the External Authentication in Control Tower

Now we move to SAP Build. From the Lobby, open Control Tower > External Authentication. This is where BPA stores the OAuth client details for the tenant. The screenshot below already shows one entry, Google Workspace Test, along with the Create New Authentication button.

 

Control Tower > External Authentication.

  1. Choose Google as the type of external portal, then enter a unique Name (this is the name you'll select in the automation later) and an optional Description.
  2. Paste the Client ID and Client Secret from the Google client (the clientid.json values).
  3. Select the scopes. User Email is pre-selected and mandatory. The list also offers Calendar, Cloud Platform, Drive and Gmail. I selected only Gmail for now, so the consent screen stays short and the permissions stay minimal. You can always create another authentication later with more scopes.

 

The Create Authentication dialog for Google.

Step 3: Register It on the Desktop Agent

The authentication exists on the tenant, but it isn't usable until the Desktop Agent on your machine registers it.

  1. In the Desktop Agent, click the Settings gear and choose External Authentication.

 

Desktop Agent --- Settings > External Authentication.

  1. The tenant's authentications are listed with their type and status. Open the one you created.

 

The external authentication listed in the Desktop Agent.

  1. Enter the email address of the Google account to use. You can mark the authentication as Default, so automations fall back to it when no name is given. Once it shows Registered, it can also be unregistered from this same screen.

 

The registered authentication, with the email address hidden.

Registering opens Google's sign-in flow in the browser. The first screen confirms which account is signing in to the app we named on the Branding page.

 

Sign in with Google --- confirming the account for SAP-BPA-Test.

The second screen lists what the app wants to access, which here is the Gmail permission we selected in Control Tower. Because the app is in Testing and unverified, Google's wording is a bit more cautious. Review it and click Continue.

 

The consent screen requesting Gmail access.

That's the whole one-time setup. Any automation running on this Desktop Agent can now use the registered Google account.

Step 4: Build the Task Automation

With authorization in place, we can build the automation itself. I added a task automation, InvoiceApprovalAutomation, to the same project that holds the invoice approval process. For this post the flow is deliberately small: authenticate, search the inbox, clean the target folder, download the attachments, and log the result.

The Test Email

To test, I sent myself an email with a recognizable subject, Gmail-BPA, and three invoice PDFs attached. The automation searches for exactly that subject, so it only picks up emails meant for it.

 

The test email in the Gmail inbox --- three PDF attachments, ready to be read by the Desktop Agent.

Building the Flow

  1. Select Google Authentication. The first activity takes the name of the external authentication as its only input. Pick the one you registered (in my case, Google Workspace Test). If it's left empty, the default registered authentication is used. The activity can throw a GoogleAuthError.

 

Select Google Authentication --- the name of the registered external authentication.

  1. Try / Catch. Everything that talks to Gmail sits inside a Try block that catches GmailError, so a failure (an expired token, for example) can be handled and logged rather than crashing the automation halfway.

 

The Try block, catching GmailError.

  1. Search Emails (Gmail). The query is Label: Inbox subject:("Gmail-BPA"), which looks in the inbox for messages with our keyword in the subject. The usual Gmail search operators work here, so you can narrow it further (for example with is:unread or has:attachment). includeSpamTrash is set to false, and the output, messageIdentifiers, is the list of matches.

 

Search Emails (Gmail) --- query on the inbox label and subject.

  1. Email Found? A Condition step checks messageIdentifiers.length > 0. If at least one email matches, the flow continues. Otherwise, the default branch just logs that nothing was found, which is a normal outcome for a scheduled run on an empty inbox.

 

The Email Found? condition.

  1. Delete All Files. Before downloading, this activity empties the target folder (GmailFileFromAgent in my case), so attachments from earlier runs aren't picked up by extraction a second time.

 

Delete All Files --- clearing the target folder before each run.

  1. Read Email (Gmail). This downloads the message. messageId is set to messageIdentifiers[0].messageId (the first match), location is fileSystem so the attachments are written to disk (the alternative is Google Drive), and pathOrDriveId is the folder we just cleaned. markAsRead is optional, and the output messageDetail holds the email details.

 

Read Email (Gmail) --- saving the attachments to the file system.

Running It

I ran the automation from the designer in unattended mode. The test console shows each step completing in order (Select Google Authentication, Search Emails, Delete All Files, Read Email, Log Message, End), and the target folder now holds the three PDF attachments from the test email.

 

The test run, with the three invoice PDFs saved into the target folder.

The greyed-out steps lower in the flow (Get File Collection, the For Each loop, DocAI - Extract with Schema and InvoiceApprovalProcess) are disabled for this run. They're the extraction and approval part from the earlier posts, which is where this folder gets used next.

Things to Keep in Mind

  • One email per run. Because the message ID comes from index 0, this flow handles the first matching email. If several invoice emails can arrive between runs, loop over messageIdentifiers and use markAsRead so each is handled once.
  • Testing-mode token expiry. For an External app in Testing status, Google limits how long a refresh token stays valid (documented as seven days). If the automation asks for authorization again after about a week, register the authentication on the Desktop Agent again. Publishing the app avoids this, but brings Google's verification process into play, especially for the Gmail scope.
  • Test users only. If Google blocks the sign-in, check that your account is on the Test users list.
  • Scopes. If Gmail calls fail with permission errors, check that the Gmail scope was selected in the External Authentication, then unregister and register again so the new scope is granted.

Wrapping Up

Connecting BPA to Gmail takes a few moving parts: a Google OAuth client, an External Authentication in Control Tower, a registration on the Desktop Agent, and one activity in the automation. Once that's done, it's a reusable foundation. The same setup can later send emails (for example approval replies), change labels on processed mails, or work with Drive and Calendar if you add those scopes.

With invoice PDFs now landing in a folder straight from an inbox, the next step is to switch the extraction and approval steps back on, so that an email arriving in Gmail ends up as an approval task in My Inbox, and the decision goes back out by email, all from within the task automation.

entry.title: Every Gmail Activity in SAP Build Process Automation: Search, Read, Label, Send, Reply and Delete
entry.content:
A hands-on walkthrough of the Gmail activities in the Google Workspace SDK, built into a single task automation and tested against real emails.

Introduction

This is the fifth post in the series. In the previous post, we set up the Google OAuth client, created the External Authentication in Control Tower, registered it on the Desktop Agent, and built a small automation that searches Gmail and saves attachments to a local folder. That post ended with one search, one read, and a folder of PDFs.

Gmail offers a lot more than that. In this post we go through every Gmail activity BPA provides, one at a time, inside a single task automation. Along the way we make sure an email is never read twice, send a fresh email with attachments, reply to a thread, and finally delete an email.

Here's what we'll cover:

  • Searching Gmail and reading an email, with its attachments saved to a local folder
  • Moving a processed email from Inbox to a "read" label, so it's never fetched again
  • Sending an email with attachments
  • Replying and replying to all on an existing thread
  • Deleting an email (and why that one deserves extra care)
  • Cleaning up with Disconnect (Google)

The Gmail Activities at a Glance

With the Google Workspace SDK added to the project, searching for "Gmail" in the automation's Tools panel lists seven activities: Send Email, Search Emails, Read Email, Modify Email Labels, Send Reply, Reply All and Delete Email. It also lists the supporting data types, such as Gmail Attachments, Gmail Message Detail, Gmail Message Identifier, Gmail Parameters and Gmail Reply Parameters. Every activity we use in this post is highlighted below in red.

 

The finished automation with each Gmail activity highlighted, next to the Gmail activities in the Tools panel.

The flow reads top to bottom, and each group of steps maps to one part of this post:

  • Steps 3 to 6: search the inbox, check that something was found, empty the target folder, and read the email with its attachments.
  • Step 7: modify the labels on the email we just read.
  • Step 8: send a new email with attachments.
  • Steps 10 to 12: search for a thread, then reply to all and reply to it.
  • Steps 13 and 14: search for a temporary email and delete it.
  • Step 15: disconnect from Google.

Everything from step 1 (Select Google Authentication) sits inside the same Try / Catch pattern from the previous post, catching GmailError.

Before You Start

  • The External Authentication from the previous post needs the Gmail scope. That scope covers reading, sending and permanently deleting email, so nothing extra is needed for this post. If you ever add a scope, update the External Authentication in Control Tower and register it on the Desktop Agent again.
  • Create a Gmail label named BPA-Read manually in Gmail. The automation applies this label but does not create it.
  • Prepare three test emails with distinct subjects, so each part of the flow only touches its own email: Gmail-BPA (with three PDF attachments) for read and label, BPA-Gmail (a thread with a few participants) for the reply steps, and BPA-Delete for the delete step.
  • Use a test mailbox. The delete step is permanent.

Part 1: Search and Read an Email

This part repeats the idea from the previous post, so I'll keep it brief. The test email sits in the Inbox, with the subject Gmail-BPA and three invoice PDFs attached.

 

The test email in the Inbox, with three PDF attachments.

  1. Search Emails (Gmail). I renamed this step "Search Emails (Gmail) for Read & Get Attachments" so it's easy to tell apart from the other searches later in the flow. The query is Label: Inbox subject:("Gmail-BPA"), so only emails still in the Inbox with that subject are returned. includeSpamTrash is false, and the output, messageIdentifiers, is the list of matches.

 

Search Emails (Gmail) for Read & Get Attachments.

  1. Email Found? A Condition step checks Step3.messageIdentifiers.length > 0. If nothing matches, the default branch just logs a message.

 

The Email Found? condition.

  1. Delete All Files. Before downloading, this empties the local target folder, so files from an earlier run are never picked up again.

 

Delete All Files on the target folder.

  1. Read Email (Gmail). messageId is messageIdentifiers[0].messageId, location is fileSystem, and pathOrDriveId is the same target folder. The three PDFs are saved there, and the output messageDetail holds the email details.

 

Read Email (Gmail) saving the three attachments into the target folder.

Part 2: Modify Email Labels

Here is a problem with the flow so far: the email stays in the Inbox after we read it, so the next run would find and read it again. We solve that with Modify Email Labels (Gmail), which moves the email out of the Inbox and into our BPA-Read label. Because the search query includes Label: Inbox, an email that has been moved never matches again.

  1. Modify Email Labels (Gmail). messageId is messageIdentifiers[0].messageId, the same email we just read. labelsToAdd is a list holding BPA-Read, and labelsToRemove is a list holding Inbox. Both lists are entered as custom data, one string per label.

 

Modify Email Labels (Gmail) adding BPA-Read and removing Inbox.

Back in Gmail, the same email now carries the BPA-Read label instead of Inbox.

 

The processed email, now labelled BPA-Read.

This is the label approach I chose over the markAsRead option on Read Email. The email keeps its read or unread state, and the label gives you a visible record of what the automation has handled, which you can also search on in Gmail.

Part 3: Send Email

Next we send a new email using Send Email (Gmail). All its inputs live in one custom data object called gmailParameters.

  1. Fill in the recipient fields: to, plus optional cc and bcc (semicolon separated). I sent it to my own address for the test.
  2. Set the subject ([BPA Auto] Invoice Attachments | Send Mail) and the body. isHtmlBody is false here, so the body is plain text. Set it to true if you want to send HTML.

 

Send Email (Gmail) --- recipients, subject, body and the start of the attachments list.

  1. Add attachments. Each attachment is its own entry with attachFrom (fileSystem here) and a filePath. I attached the same three PDFs we downloaded in Part 1, purely for convenience. Any file path works, so you can attach whatever your scenario needs.

 

One attachment entry per file, each with attachFrom and filePath.

The email arrives with all three PDFs attached.

 

The email sent by the automation, with its three attachments.

Part 4: Reply and Reply All

To reply to an existing conversation, the automation needs to know which thread to reply into. For this I set up a separate test thread with a few participants, subject BPA-Gmail, and added a dedicated search step for it.

  1. Search Emails (Gmail) To Reply. The query is Label: Inbox subject:("BPA-Gmail"), and the output is again messageIdentifiers, this time from step 10.

 

Search Emails (Gmail) To Reply.

  1. Reply All (Gmail). The input is replyParamters (the spelling as it appears in the activity). threadId is messageIdentifiers[0].threadId from step 10, which is what places the reply inside the existing conversation. messageId, to, cc and bcc are left empty, and the body is the text to send. includeOriginalAttachments is false, and attachments can be added the same way as in Send Email.

 

Reply All (Gmail), with threadId taken from the search step.

  1. Send Reply (Gmail). It has the same parameters as Reply All. The difference is in who receives the message: Reply All goes to everyone on the thread, while Send Reply goes back to a single recipient.

 

Send Reply (Gmail), with the same parameter structure.

In Gmail, both messages show up inside the original thread. In my test, the Reply All message went to all four other participants, and the Reply went to one.

 

The test thread, with the Reply All and Reply messages sent by the automation at the bottom.

Part 5: Delete Email

The last activity is Delete Email (Gmail). As with replying, we first find the email, this time using a dedicated search step with the subject BPA-Delete.

  1. Search Emails (Gmail) To Delete. The query is Label: Inbox subject:("BPA-Delete"), and the output messageIdentifiers comes from step 13.

 

Search Emails (Gmail) To Delete.

  1. Delete Email (Gmail). The only required input is messageId, here messageIdentifiers[0].messageId from step 13.

 

Delete Email (Gmail) with the messageId from the search step.

This is the temporary email the automation removes:

 

The temporary email, before the automation runs.

This deletion is permanent. When you delete an email in the Gmail interface, it moves to Trash and is removed later, either after Gmail's retention period or when you empty the Trash yourself. The Delete Email activity does not do that. In my test the email was gone immediately and did not appear in Trash, which matches how Google describes the underlying delete call in the Gmail API: immediate and permanent, with no way to undo it. Treat this activity like a delete statement without a rollback.

Finishing Up: Disconnect (Google)

The last step of the flow, step 15, is Disconnect (Google), which closes the connection to Google once the work is done. It sits after the Try / Catch block, so it runs on both the success and error paths.

Things to Keep in Mind

  • Be careful with delete. Use a precise query (here, a keyword unique to the temporary email), run it against a test mailbox first, and consider whether a label like BPA-Delete or a separate review step is safer for production scenarios.
  • Guard the later steps. In this flow, steps 10 to 14 sit outside the Email Found? condition, and they read messageIdentifiers[0]. If a search returns no results, that step has nothing to read. Wrapping each search-then-act pair in its own condition, like we did for step 4, avoids that.
  • First match only. Using index 0 means each run handles one email per search. For several emails, loop over messageIdentifiers.
  • Labels must exist. Modify Email Labels uses the label names you enter, so create BPA-Read in Gmail first and keep the spelling identical.
  • Gmail search syntax. The query field accepts the same operators as the Gmail search bar, so you can narrow results further (for example, by sender or date).
  • Testing-mode token expiry. As noted in the previous post, an External app in Testing status has a limited refresh token lifetime. If authorization suddenly fails after about a week, register the authentication on the Desktop Agent again.

Wrapping Up

With these seven activities, a BPA automation can do nearly everything you'd do by hand in a Gmail inbox: find an email, read it and save its attachments, mark it as processed, send a new message, reply into a thread, and, when needed, delete one for good. They all run on the single setup from the previous post.

If you want to take this further into a complete invoice flow, you can combine the pieces from this series yourself. Each post covers one layer: the first builds the invoice approval process, the second sets up Document AI extraction on a trial instance, the third wires extraction into the approval process, and the fourth connects BPA to Google Workspace and fetches the attachments. This post adds the remaining Gmail activities on top of that setup. The fetched PDFs from the Gmail steps can serve as the source folder for the extraction automation in the second and third posts.

Each part is covered and tested on its own, and the connection points (a folder of PDFs, then extraction, then a call to the approval process) are the same ones those posts already use. If you would like the decision to go back to the sender as a reply in the original email thread, the Send Reply and Reply All activities are the ones to look at. The approval emails in the earlier posts are sent from the process itself, so that part would need some extra wiring.

entry.title: Working with Google Drive in SAP Build Process Automation: Find, Move and Rename Files
entry.content:
A hands-on walkthrough of the Google Drive activities in the Google Workspace SDK: searching for folders and files, moving a file into another folder, and renaming it.

Introduction

This is the sixth post in the series. The fourth post covered the one-time setup for Google Workspace: the OAuth client in Google Cloud Console, the External Authentication in Control Tower, and registering it on the Desktop Agent. The fifth used that setup to go through the Gmail activities. This post uses the same foundation for Google Drive.

Drive is a natural companion to Gmail. Attachments, invoices and reports often end up in Drive folders, and an automation needs to find them, organise them and sometimes rename them. We build one task automation that does exactly that, and along the way look at how the query field works, since it's what makes the search activities flexible.

Here's what we'll cover:

  • Listing folders and files, with and without a query
  • Finding a folder or file by name
  • Moving a file into a folder and renaming it, using IDs returned by the earlier steps
  • Writing Drive search queries

The Google Drive activity group is larger than what we use here. This post covers six of its activities, plus Select Google Authentication and Disconnect (Google).

The Drive Activities at a Glance

Searching for "drive" in the Tools panel lists the Google Drive activities: Rename File, Move File, Get Folder By Name, Get File By Name, Get File, Get Folder, Download File, Share To Email, Share To Domain, Share With Anyone, Delete File Or Folder and Upload File. The six highlighted in red are the ones used in this post, and they are all visible in the flow on the left.

 

The automation flow with the six Drive activities highlighted, next to the Google Drive activities in the Tools panel.

The flow is a straight line with no branches:

  • Step 1: Select Google Authentication.
  • Steps 2 to 5: Get Folder, twice (once without a query, once with one).
  • Steps 6 and 7: Get Folder By Name.
  • Steps 8 to 11: Get File, and Get File By Name.
  • Steps 12 to 15: Move File, then Rename File.
  • Step 16: Disconnect (Google).

Almost every activity is followed by a Log Message step that prints the activity's output, so we can see in the test console what Drive returned. All the Drive activities return their results in an output called metaDatas (or a simple true result for move and rename), and the number in front of it in the screenshots is the step that produced it.

Before You Start

  • Complete the setup from the fourth post. In Google Cloud Console, the Google Drive API must be enabled and the Drive scope added under Data Access.
  • In Control Tower, the External Authentication you select must include the Drive scope. The authentication in the fourth post only selected Gmail, so add Drive, then register the authentication on the Desktop Agent again so Google's consent screen asks for Drive access too.
  • The Drive scope gives access to all files in the Drive of the account you sign in with, so use a test account for experiments like this one.

For the test I created a Drive folder named SAP BPA TEST holding a few invoice PDFs, and, inside it, an empty folder named BPA Moved File that will receive the moved file. This is the Drive before the automation runs:

 

The SAP BPA TEST folder before the run: the empty BPA Moved File folder and three PDFs.

Part 1: Get Folder

Get Folder (Google Drive) searches for folders. It has three optional inputs: driveId (to target a specific drive), query, and timeout. The output, metaDatas, is the list of folders found.

  1. Get Folder without a query. I left all inputs empty. In my test, this returned every folder in my Drive.

 

Get Folder (Google Drive) with no query.

  1. Get Folder Log. A Log Message step takes metaDatas from step 2 as its message. I show this log step only once, because every other log step in the flow works the same way. The full list of folders it prints is long, so I'm not including that output.

 

Log Message printing the metaDatas output of step 2.

  1. Get Folder with a query. The second Get Folder step narrows the search with this query: mimeType = 'application/vnd.google-apps.folder' and name contains 'SAP'. It returns folders whose names contain a word starting with SAP.

 

Get Folder (Google Drive) - 2 with a query.

The log of this step (step 5) shows what came back: the SAP BPA TEST folder, with its ID, creation time and modification time. The IDs are hidden in the screenshot.

 

Log output of step 5: the matching folder.

Writing Drive Queries

The query field follows Google's Drive search query syntax, the same one the Drive API uses. A query has three parts: a term to search on, an operator, and a value, and parts can be combined with and, or, and not. Google's search query reference lists all valid terms and operators. These are the ones I find most useful:

  • name contains 'SAP' matches items whose name has a word beginning with SAP.
  • name = 'BPA_Demo_Invoice.pdf' matches an exact name.
  • mimeType = 'application/vnd.google-apps.folder' matches folders only. For PDFs, use mimeType = 'application/pdf'.
  • mimeType = 'application/pdf' and name contains 'Invoice' combines two conditions.
  • 'FOLDER_ID' in parents and trashed = false lists items directly inside a folder, excluding items in the Trash. Replace FOLDER_ID with the folder's ID.
  • modifiedTime > '2026-10-01T00:00:00' matches items modified after a date (RFC 3339 format).
  • fullText contains 'invoice' searches names, descriptions and the indexed content of files.

A few rules worth knowing:

  • Values go in single quotes. A single quote inside a value must be escaped with a backslash, for example name contains 'Bob\'s'.
  • name contains only matches the beginning of words. Google's example: for an item named HelloWorld, name contains 'Hello' finds it, but name contains 'World' does not.
  • To leave out items in the Trash, add trashed = false.

In this post I tested the name and mimeType terms. The other terms are documented by Google for the Drive API, but I'd recommend trying them in a test folder first.

Part 2: Get Folder By Name

When you only know a folder's name, Get Folder By Name (Google Drive) is simpler than writing a query. Its required input is name, which I set to BPA Moved File. The name doesn't have to be complete; in my tests a partial name matched as well.

 

Get Folder By Name (Google Drive) with the folder name.

The log of step 7 shows one folder returned: BPA Moved File. Its ID is what the Move File step uses later.

 

Log output of step 7: the BPA Moved File folder.

Part 3: Get File and Get File By Name

Files have their own pair of activities. Get File (Google Drive) has the same inputs as Get Folder (driveId, query, timeout) and returns files. With no query it returns files from the whole Drive, so I don't show its log, which is a long list.

 

Get File (Google Drive) with no query.

Get File By Name (Google Drive) takes a required fileName. I used BPA_Demo, a partial name, so it matches every file whose name starts that way.

 

Get File By Name (Google Drive) with a partial file name.

Because the name was partial, the log of step 11 lists several files: BPA_Demo_Invoice.pdf, BPA_Demo_Invoice_Approval_01.pdf and BPA_Demo_Invoice_AutoApproval_02.pdf. In this run, the first item in the list was BPA_Demo_Invoice.pdf, which is the file I want to move.

 

Log output of step 11: the files matching the partial name.

Part 4: Move File

Move File (Google Drive) needs two IDs, both taken from earlier steps:

  • fileId: metaDatas[0].id from step 10, the first file returned by Get File By Name.
  • destinationFolderId: metaDatas[0].id from step 6, the folder returned by Get Folder By Name.

The two steps that provide the IDs are marked in red in the flow. The output result is true when the move succeeded.

 

Move File (Google Drive), with its two IDs coming from steps 10 and 6.

Part 5: Rename File

Rename File (Google Drive) takes fileId and newName. A move doesn't change a file's ID, so I reuse metaDatas[0].id from step 10 and rename the file to Moved_File.pdf. Include the extension in the new name, because the name you enter is the whole name.

 

Rename File (Google Drive), reusing the file ID from step 10.

The logs for steps 13 and 15 simply print the true result of Move File and Rename File:

 

Move File Log and Rename File Log, both printing true.

Finishing Up: Disconnect (Google)

The last step, Disconnect (Google), closes the connection to Google when the work is done.

Running It

I ran the automation from the designer. The test console prints the results of each log step. Some entries are hidden, because they contain names and IDs from my Drive. The final two entries are the true results of Move File and Rename File. The warning at the end only says the testing session has stopped.

 

The test console, with IDs and some names hidden.

In Drive, BPA_Demo_Invoice.pdf is no longer in the SAP BPA TEST folder:

 

The SAP BPA TEST folder after the run.

Inside the BPA Moved File folder, the file is now called Moved_File.pdf:

 

The BPA Moved File folder after the run, holding the renamed file.

Things to Keep in Mind

  • Check which item you take from the list. Partial names can match several items, and the steps above use metaDatas[0], the first one. Here the first match was the file I wanted, but I wouldn't rely on the order. Use a more specific name or query, or look through metaDatas for the item you need.
  • Guard against empty results. If a search finds nothing, a later step that reads metaDatas[0] has nothing to read. Add a condition after each search, as in the Gmail posts.
  • Add error handling. These activities can throw a GoogleDriveError. I left out Try / Catch to keep the flow readable, but you should wrap the Drive steps in one in a real automation.
  • Avoid logging full lists. Get Folder and Get File without a query return everything they can find, which makes long logs in a large Drive. Use a query to narrow results.
  • Treat logs as sensitive. They include file and folder IDs, and for files, download links. Hide them in screenshots you share.
  • Test-mode token expiry. As mentioned in the fourth post, an External app in Testing status has a limited refresh token lifetime. If authorization fails after about a week, register the authentication on the Desktop Agent again.

Wrapping Up

With a handful of activities, a BPA automation can search a Drive by name or by query, organise files into folders and rename them, all driven by the IDs that earlier steps return. The same Google setup from the fourth post serves both Gmail and Drive. The other Drive activities in the Tools panel (Download, Share, Delete and Upload) aren't covered in this post.
